Figures 4.30 and 4.31 (pictures of collagen, haemoglobin and body proteins) are covered in the text.

blocks.text: The most abundant organic compounds in the cell are proteins. They may be defined as the polymers of amino acids and are regarded as the principal compounds of cells. J. J. Berzelius coined the term "protein" (from the Greek proteios, molecules of the first rank) to emphasise the importance of this group of macromolecules. Proteins are important for the structures of cells and organisms and participate in everything they do; in this way they act as the building blocks of life.

blocks.title: Diversity
blocks.text: The diversity of the biological world is the reflection of the diversity of structure and function that exists in proteins.
Structure of proteins
Proteins are polymers formed by the interlinkage of monomers called amino acids. Different proteins may have from a few to 3000 amino acids: insulin has 51 amino acids, haemoglobin 574.
Amino acid

The amino acid is the basic structural unit of proteins. It is an organic molecule in which four groups, an amino group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen (H) and a side group (R), are attached to the same carbon atom, the alpha carbon.

blocks.alt: The alpha carbon at the centre bonded to four groups drawn as lobes: H2N (amino group) on the left, COOH (carboxyl group) on the right, R (side group) above and H below.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.23: Structure of an amino acid (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.23).

blocks.text: Although many different amino acids occur in nature, about 170 types have been reported in living organisms (in cells and tissues); of these about 25 may take part as building units of proteins, and most proteins are made of 20 types. The identity and unique chemical properties of each amino acid are determined by the nature of its side group (R), covalently bonded to the alpha carbon: R may be a hydrogen atom, as in glycine, or CH3, as in alanine, or any other group.

blocks.alt: Two amino acids side by side: glycine (green), whose central carbon carries H2N, COOH, H and H (R = H); and alanine (blue), whose central carbon carries H2N, COOH, CH3 and H (R = CH3).
blocks.caption: Figure 4.24: General structures of glycine and alanine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.24).

blocks.title: Essential and non-essential amino acids
blocks.text: Of the 20 amino acids, our bodies can make eleven, the non-essential amino acids: alanine, arginine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, proline, serine and tyrosine. The remaining nine cannot be made by our bodies and must be obtained from food; these essential amino acids are methionine, valine, tryptophan, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, threonine, phenylalanine and histidine (necessary only for babies).
The peptide bond

A covalent bond that links two amino acids is a peptide bond. Each amino acid has an amino group at one end and a carboxyl group at the other. When two amino acids are brought close, dehydration synthesis occurs between the amino group of one and the carboxyl group of the second, releasing a molecule of water and forming a peptide bond between the N and the C of the adjacent amino acids. Amino acids linked by peptide bonds are peptides; a dipeptide forms from two amino acids, for example glycylalanine from glycine and alanine. A dipeptide still has an amino group at one end and a carboxyl group at the other, so both reactive parts are available for further peptide bonds, and the addition of amino acids ultimately gives polypeptide chains.

blocks.alt: Glycine + Alanine; an arrow down releases H2O and gives glycylalanine: H2N-CH2-C(=O)-N(H)-CH(CH3)-COOH, the C(=O) part green (from glycine) and the N-H part blue (from alanine), the C-N bond between them red and labelled Peptide bond. Labels: Glycine, Alanine, H2O, Glycylalanine, Peptide bond.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.25: Formation of peptide bond between glycine and alanine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.25).

blocks.text: A protein is composed of one or more polypeptide chains: insulin contains two polypeptide chains, haemoglobin four. Polypeptide chains assume different shapes on the basis of the number, types and sequence of their amino acids, which gives proteins different levels of structure.

blocks.alt: A chain H2N-C-C-N-C-C-N-C-C-N-C-COOH: each alpha carbon carries R above and H below, each carbonyl carbon a double-bonded O above, each N an H above; the C-N bond between the first carbonyl carbon and the next N is labelled Peptide bond.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.26: Section from a polypeptide chain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.26).

blocks.text: Structural levels of proteins

The diversity of proteins ranges from simpler proteins, consisting of linear chains of amino acids, to complex proteins with structural modifications of the linear chains. Proteins are built at the following levels.
Primary structure

The primary structure of a protein is formed by the linear arrangement of amino acids: it represents the number and sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. All protein molecules, simple or complex, have specific primary structures. The primary structure of insulin reveals two polypeptide chains, the smaller alpha chain of 21 amino acids and the longer beta chain of 30. Similarly, the primary structure of haemoglobin shows four polypeptide chains: two alpha chains of 141 amino acids each and two beta chains of 146 each.

blocks.alt: Two bead chains: the A chain (21 red beads) above and the longer B chain (30 green beads) below, bending at its end. Cysteine beads are marked Cys; dashed S-S bonds join A6 to A11 within the A chain, and A7 to B7 and A20 to B19 between the chains. Legend: S-S bonds, A Chain, B Chain.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.27: Chains of Insulin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.27).

blocks.title: Over 10,000 proteins
blocks.text: There are over 10,000 proteins in the human body, and each has its specific primary structure: a specific number, sequence and types of amino acids.

The number, sequence and types of amino acids in the primary structure of a protein are highly specific, for its proper functioning. This specificity is determined by the order of nucleotides in DNA. Any change results in an abnormal protein that fails to carry out its normal function. For example, sickle cell haemoglobin is formed by a mistake in the arrangement of only one amino acid, at position six in each beta chain, where valine is present in place of glutamic acid. Because of sickle cell haemoglobin, red blood cells get sickle shapes and the abnormal haemoglobin cannot transport sufficient oxygen. This disease is sickle cell anaemia.

blocks.alt: Two rows of seven linked boxes. Normal haemoglobin: Valine, Histidine, Leucine, Threonine, Proline, Glutamic acid, Glutamic acid, with an arrow to a round normal red blood cell. Sickle cell haemoglobin: the same except the sixth box, Valine (highlighted), with an arrow to a sickle-shaped red blood cell.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.28: Difference in amino acid sequence in normal and sickle cell haemoglobin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.28).

blocks.text: Secondary structure

In many proteins, folding or coiling patterns occur within a polypeptide chain; this is the secondary structure. Coiling of a polypeptide chain gives an alpha helix, while folding makes a pleated sheet. Both structures are maintained by hydrogen bonds between the amino and carboxyl groups of nearby amino acids in the chain.
Tertiary structure

When the secondary structure folds up further and takes a complicated globular shape, this is the tertiary structure; these are more complex proteins. The globular shape is maintained by ionic, hydrogen and disulphide bonds, which contribute to the overall stability and shape of the protein. The amino acids of a polypeptide chain interact with water to give the most stable tertiary structure, a globular shape, through hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions: the hydrophobic (non-polar) amino acids aggregate in a way that disrupts the hydrogen bonding of water molecules and so are buried inside, while the hydrophilic (polar) amino acids turn outwards, towards the surface of the water.
Quaternary structure

When two or more polypeptide chains with tertiary structures are held together by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds, they form the most complex proteins. This aggregation of tertiary structures is the quaternary structure of a protein.

blocks.alt: Primary structure (a chain of amino acid beads) -> secondary structure as an alpha helix and as a pleated sheet -> tertiary structure (a folded chain containing a helix and a sheet) -> quaternary structure (four folded chains packed together), joined by arrows. Labels: Primary structure, Secondary structure (alpha helix), Secondary structure (pleated sheet), Tertiary structure, Alpha helix, Pleated sheet, Quaternary structure.

blocks.text: Classification of proteins

Proteins are a very diverse group and can be classified on different bases. By their role in living organisms they are structural proteins and functional proteins. The recommended classification is based on structure, as fibrous proteins and globular proteins.

rows: Soluble in salt, acid or base solutions and in aqueous alcohol
Disorganised by changes in the environment
Silk fibre (webs of silkworm and spider); actin in muscle cells; fibrin in blood clots; keratin in nails, hair, beak, skin; collagen in the matrix of connective tissues
Enzymes (biocatalysts); antibodies (active against invading antigens); some hormones (regulate the body's activities); haemoglobin (oxygen-carrying protein)

blocks.text: Role of proteins in life
Proteins carry out virtually all the activities of living organisms. Some of their remarkable structural and functional roles are these.

blocks.alt: (a) Collagen: a long straight fibre made of three bead strands (red, green, blue) twisted round each other. (b) Haemoglobin: four folded chains, two red and two yellow, packed into a compact globule.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.30: (a) Collagen - a fibrous protein, (b) haemoglobin - a globular protein (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.30).

items: Proteins are an important part of the composition of all plasma membranes. Channel proteins in cell membranes control the movement of materials in and out of cells; for example, proteins make the sodium-potassium pump in the membrane of neurons, which controls the movement of Na+ and K+ ions in and out of the nerve cell.
Some fibrous proteins, for example collagen and keratin, make almost the whole structure of cartilage, and of hair and nails respectively.
Enzymes are a class of proteins that catalyse the metabolism of cells, a very diverse class: proteases catalyse the breakdown of proteins, polymerases the synthesis of polymers.

Some very important animal hormones are proteins or peptides: insulin (controls blood glucose level), antidiuretic hormone (increases water retention by the kidneys) and oxytocin (regulates milk production).

Some globular proteins transport materials through the body: haemoglobin and myoglobin transport oxygen and some carbon dioxide, and cytochromes work in the electron transport chain as electron carriers.
Albumin is a blood protein that maintains the osmotic concentration of blood and keeps its ability to flow.
Blood clotting prevents the loss of blood after an injury. The protein fibrinogen is present in blood; when an injury occurs it is activated into fibrin, which makes fibres, and a clot forms.
All contractions in living matter are due to proteins: actin and myosin, the main proteins of muscles, are responsible for muscular contraction, and tubulin makes spindle fibres.
Antibodies recognise and combine with foreign substances (antigens) and convert them into harmless products.
Some ion-binding proteins store ions in different parts of the body: ferritin is the main intracellular iron storage protein, and casein, a milk protein, stores potassium and calcium ions.
Repressors are proteins that regulate gene action by preventing the synthesis of RNA, allowing genes to work where and when required.

blocks.title: Ferritin as a test
blocks.text: Blood ferritin levels are measured in patients as a diagnostic tool for anaemia. If ferritin is high there is iron in excess; if it is low there is a risk of iron shortage, which sooner or later could lead to anaemia.
